div.p: We consider an extended spatial autoregressive model that can incorporate possible endogenous interactions, exogenous interactions, unobserved group fixed effects and the correlation of unobservables. In the generalized method of moments (GMM) and the maximum likelihood (ML) frameworks, we introduce simple gradient-based robust test statistics that can be used to test for the presence of the endogenous effects, the correlation of unobservables and the contextual effects. These test statistics are robust to local parametric misspecifications and only require consistent estimates from a transformed linear regression model to compute. We carry out an extensive Monte Carlo study to investigate the size and power properties of the proposed tests. The results show that the proposed tests have good finite sample properties, and are useful for testing the presence of the various effects in a social interaction model.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: In a social interaction model, an individual's outcome is affected by the outcomes and the characteristics of the reference group's members, i.e., the peers. The effects channelled through the outcomes of the reference group's members are known as the endogenous effects, and the effects arising from the characteristics of the reference group's members are called the contextual effects. Identification of these effects within an estimation framework is important because their policy implications greatly differ. Manski (1993) shows that endogenous and contextual effects cannot be separately identified in a linear-in-means model. This identification problem, known as the 'reflection problem', has led to various adjustments to the linear-in-means specification to allow for partial or full identification of these effects (Bramoullé, Djebbari, & Fortin, 2009;Brock & Durlauf, 2001;Burridge, Elhorst, & Zigova, 2016;Calvo-Armengol, Patacchini, & Zenou, 2009;Goldsmith-Pinkham & Imbens, 2013;Hsieh & Lee, 2016;Lee, 2007;Lin, 2010;Liu & Lee, 2010).

Tools from spatial econometrics can be used to reformulate social interaction models in such a way that identification of various effects becomes available. For spatial econometric models, see, for example, Anselin (1988), LeSage and Pace (2009), and Elhorst (2010Elhorst ( , 2014)). The group relation can be represented by means of a so-called spatial weights (or connectivity) matrix. The outcomes of a group's members are included in the model through a so-called spatial lag operator which constructs a new variable consisting of a weighted average of the group members' outcomes. Similarly, the contextual effects are formulated through a spatial lag of the group members' characteristics. This class of models is referred to as social interaction models with network structures (Lee, 2007;Lee, Liu, & Lin, 2010;Liu, Patacchini, & Zenou, 2014).

In the literature, diagnostic testing procedures for social interaction models with network structures have received scant attention. Gradient or score-based tests within the generalized method of moments (GMM) or maximum likelihood (ML) frameworks can be formulated to test the presence of various effects by following White (1982), Newey (1985aNewey ( , 1985b)), Tauchen (1985), Newey and West (1987) and Smith (1987). However, these gradient-based tests (i.e., the Lagrange multiplier (LM) tests) are not robust to local parametric misspecifications in the alternative model. Within the ML framework, Davidson and MacKinnon (1987), Saikkonen (1989), and Bera and Yoon (1993) show that the conventional LM test statistic has a non-central chisquare distribution when the alternative hypothesis deviates (locally) from the true data-generating process (DGP). Bera, Montes-Rojas, and Sosa-Escudero (2010) extend this result to a GMM framework and show that the asymptotic distribution of the LM test is a non-central chi-square distribution when the alternative model deviates locally from the true DGP. Thus, conventional LM tests will over-reject the true null hypothesis, and will lead to incorrect inference under a parametric misspecification scenario. Bera and Yoon (1993) and Bera et al. (2010) formulate robust (or adjusted) tests that asymptotically have a central chi-square distribution irrespective of the local deviation of the alternative model from the true DGP.

In this paper, we formulate robust LM tests in the GMM and ML frameworks for a social interaction model with a network structure. We derive the asymptotic distribution of these tests under the null and the local alternatives within the context of our social interaction model. These tests can be used to detect the presence of the endogenous effects, correlation of unobservables and the contextual effects. Besides being robust to local parametric misspecifications in the alternative model, these tests are computationally very simple and only require estimates from a transformed linear regression model. We design an extensive Monte Carlo study to investigate the size and power properties of our proposed tests. Our results show that the proposed tests have good finite sample properties and can be useful for the identification of the source of dependence in a social interaction model.

The paper is organized as follows. The next section introduces the social interaction model. The third section reviews the GMM estimation approach and introduces the GMM gradient tests for testing linear and nonlinear restrictions on the spatial autoregressive parameters. We adjust these procedures for our social interaction model and formulate the robust LM test statistics. The fourth section considers the ML estimation approach for the model and formulates various versions of the LM tests. The fifth section introduces test statistics for testing the presence of contextual effects in both GMM and ML frameworks. The sixth section shows the relationships between the test statistics. The seventh to ninth sections compare the size and power properties of tests through a Monte Carlo study. The tenth section concludes. Some technical details are relegated to Appendices A-D in the supplemental data available online.

div.head: THE MODEL SPECIFICATION
div.p: We consider a group interaction setting that consists of R groups. Let m r be the number of individuals in the rth group, and n = R r=1 m r be the total number of individuals. Let Y r = (Y 1r , Y 2r , . . . , Y m r r ) ′ be the m r × 1 vector of observed outcomes in the rth group. Then the DGP stated for the rth group is given by:
div.formula: Y r = l 0 W r Y r + X 1r b 01 + W r X 2r b 02 + l m r a 0r + u r ,(1)
u r = r 0 M r u r + 1 r , for r = 1, . . . , R,(2)
div.p: where the network weights matrices W r and M r are m r × m r matrices with known constant terms and zero diagonal elements. The matrices of exogenous variables are denoted with X 1r and X 2r , which have dimensions of m r × k 1 and m r × k 2 respectively. 1 The corresponding parameter vectors for the exogenous variables are denoted by β 01 and β 02 . The endogenous social interaction effects are captured by W r Y r with the scalar coefficient λ 0 . The contextual effects are captured by W r X 2r with the matching parameter vector of β 02 . The model differs from the cross-sectional spatial econometric models by including the unobserved group fixed effects, denoted by l m r a 0r , where l m r is an m r × 1 vector of ones and a 0r represents the unobserved group fixed effects. The regression disturbance term u r = (u 1r , . . . , u m r r ) ′ and the innovation term 1 r = (1 1r , . . . , 1 m r r ) ′ are m r -dimensional vectors. The distributional assumption is imposed on the elements of ε r by assuming that 1 ir 's are i.i.d. with mean zero and variance s 2 0 . Finally, the unobserved correlated effects within the rth group are captured by M r u r with the scalar coefficient ρ 0 . In the spatial econometric literature, λ 0 and ρ 0 are called the spatial autoregressive parameters.

The network structure specified through the weights matrices W r and M r has implications for the estimation approach adopted. In Lee (2007), W r = ((1)/(m r -1))(l m r l ′ m r -I m r ) is the m r × m r network matrix, which indicates that each individual in the group is equally affected by the other members of the group. Hence, the spatial lag term W r Y r denotes the average outcome for group r. The zero diagonal property of W r indicates that Y ir is not included in the calculation of the group mean outcome for the ith individual, which is not the case in Manski (1993). The network matrices considered in Lee et al. (2010) may differ from above W r , but their rows still sum to a constant. In the case where this property is violated, the likelihood function of the model cannot be derived, and therefore Liu and Lee (2010) propose two-stage least squares (2SLS) and GMM methods for estimation.

In certain interaction scenarios, elements of the weights matrices might be a function of the sample size n. For the cross-sectional spatial autoregressive models without group fixed effects, Lee (2004) assumes a large group interaction setting and specifies elements of the weights matrix by w ij = O(1/h n ). Here, w ij is the (i, j)th element of the weights matrix W and {h n } is a sequence of real numbers that can be bounded or divergent with the property that lim n 1 h n /n = 0. For the case where W r = ((1)/(m r -1))(l m r l ′ m r -I m r ), we have h n = m r -1 and h n /n = (m r -1)/n, where n = R r=1 m r . If there is no variation in group sizes and the increase in n is generated by the increase in m r and R, then clearly lim n 1 h n /n = 0. However, as shown in Lee (2007), the endogenous effects cannot be identified in this case. In addition, Lee shows that both the endogenous and exogenous effects are weakly identified and their rates of convergence can be quite low when all group sizes are large, even if there is group size variation. Therefore, following Lee et al. (2010) and Liu and Lee (2010), we assume an interaction scenario in which {h n } is bounded.

div.head: RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN TEST STATISTICS
div.p: There are four important observations in regard to the robust tests. First, the robust tests share the optimality property of the Neyman's C(α) test (Bera & Yoon, 1993). It is important to note that the motivation for both tests are different. In the case of the robust test, the one-directional test statistic is adjusted so that it has a central chi-square distribution when the alternative model has a local parametric misspecification. On the other hand, the C(α) test is developed in a framework that involves several nuisance parameters. In such a framework, an optimal test is the one that has the highest power among the class of tests obtaining the same size. To achieve optimality, the C(α) test statistic is constructed in such a way that it is orthogonal to the gradients with respect to the nuisance parameters. The C(α) test can be computed using any consistent estimator and it reduces to the standard LM test when it is formulated from the optimal restricted GMME or the restricted MLE. Second, the robust tests are formulated by an estimator obtained under the joint null hypothesis H 0 :r 0 = r w , l 0 = l w . Under the joint null, the model reduces to a one-way panel data type model Y r = X 1r b 01 + W r X 2r b 02 + l m r a 0r + 1 r , which can be estimated by an ordinary least squares (OLS) estimator. Therefore, the computation of test statistics does not require any nonlinear optimization routines. On the other hand, the conditional LM tests (see LM jA r , LM jA l LM jA c and LM jA c , where j = g, m, in Tables 1 and 2) require the estimation of spatial parameters, which can be computationally involved.

div.head: RESULTS FOR ENDOGENOUS EFFECTS AND CORRELATED EFFECTS
div.p: In this section, we investigate the finite sample properties of the test statistics for endogenous effects and correlated effects. In the following, we first evaluate the empirical rejection frequency of each test under the null hypothesis, and then proceed to the power analysis.

div.head: Results on size properties
div.p: To present simulation results on size properties, we use the P-value discrepancy plots suggested in Davidson and MacKinnon (1998), which are based on the empirical distribution functions (edf) of p-values. Let τ be a test statistic, and τ j for j = 1, . . . , R be the R realizations of τ generated in a Monte Carlo experiment. Let F(x) be the cumulative distribution function (cdf) of the asymptotic distribution of τ evaluated at x. Then the p-value associated with τ j , denoted by p(τ j ), is given by p(τ j ) = 1-F(τ j ). An estimate of the cdf of p(τ) can be constructed simply from the edf of p(τ j ). Consider a sequence of points denoted by x i for i = 1, … , m from the interval (0, 1). As stated in Davidson and MacKinnon (1998), there is no decisive way to choose the sequence x i from (0, 1). In practice, the main attention is typically paid to the type-I errors which are set at levels smaller than or equal to 10%. We choose the following sequence and focus on levels smaller than or equal to 10%. {x i } m i=1 = {0.001:0.001:0.010 0.015:0.005:0.990 0.991:0.001:0.999} (

The P-value discrepancy plot is defined as the plot of F (x i )x i against x i under the assumption that the true DGP is characterized by the null hypothesis. If F(x) approximates the finite sample distribution of τ well enough, then each p(τ j ) will have a uniform distribution over (0, 1). Hence, the P-value plot, obtained by a plot of F (x i ) against x i , should be close to the 45°line. Therefore, a P-value discrepancy plot highlights the differences between the empirical distribution function and the 45°line. The discrepancies from the horizontal axis in a P-value discrepancy plot suggest an empirical distribution that differs from the asymptotic distribution used to determine the critical values.

To assess the significance of discrepancies in a P-value discrepancy plot, we construct a pointwise 95% confidence interval for a nominal size by using a normal approximation to the binomial distribution. Let α denote the nominal size at which the test is carried out. Using a normal approximation to the binomial distribution, a point-wise 95% confidence interval centred on α is given by a + 1.96 [a(1a)/R] 1/2 , and thus it would include rejection rates between a -1.96 [a(1a)/R] 1/2 and a + 1.96 [a(1a)/R] 1/2 . We use this approach to insert a 95% point-wise confidence interval in a P-value discrepancy plot. In the discrepancy plots, this interval will be represented by the red solid lines (for some examples, see Taṣ pınar & Doğan, 2017).

To save space, the size results based on the SLX models will be presented through the P-value discrepancy plots while the size results based on SARAR(1, 0) or SARAR(0, 1) are summarized in tables. When the null model is SARAR(1,0) or SARAR(0,1), we focus solely on the nominal size of 5% and provide size deviations at this level only.

. Figures 1 and 2 present the size properties of test statistics under H 0 :λ 0 = ρ 0 = 0. They show that all LM tests based on GMM are generally oversized regardless of the normality of the errors. In both, the maximum size distortion is always less than 0.03 and the size distortions generally lie inside the 95% point-wise confidence interval and therefore they are acceptable. . In Figure 1, LM gA r and LM gA l are generally oversized and their size discrepancies lie outside the 95% point-wise confidence interval. For example, for the nominal size of 5%, the actual rejection rate of LM gA r is about 7%. In Figure 2, LM gA l , LM gw l and LM gA r are oversized especially in panel (a). . Figures 1 and 2 clearly indicate that the size distortions of all ML-based tests generally lie inside the 95% point-wise confidence interval and are smaller compared to the GMM-based tests. Surprisingly, the ML-based tests perform in a similar fashion even when the errors are not normally distributed. . Tables 3 and 4 provide some evidence on the magnitude of size distortions as a function of the size of local parametric misspecification in the alternative model. We would expect that the robust versions of one directional tests, LM w r and LM w l , to perform relatively better than LM ρ and LM λ respectively. Overall, this seems to be the case, especially when the null model is SARAR(0, 1).
. Tables 3 and 4 show that LM A r and LM A l perform well in all cases. This is not surprising as these tests require the estimation of the spatial parameter λ 0 and ρ 0 respectively.

. When the null model is SARAR (1,0) in Tables 3 and 4, LM w r performs satisfactorily for small values of λ 0 in the alternative model. Indeed, when λ 0 is less than 0.3, LM w r always performs better than LM ρ . On the other hand, when the local misspecification deteriorates as λ 0 gets larger, LM w r severely over rejects the null model, although still beats LM ρ in all cases. Recall that LM w r uses the least squares residuals from the transformed model and implements a correction on the test statistics for a local parametric misspecification of the alternative model, i.e., ignoring the spatial lag. The bias of the least squares residuals depends on the strength of spatial dependence as well as on the connectedness of the weights matrix. Therefore, we can expect poor performance for the robust tests as λ 0 deviates from zero substantially. Note that when the null model is SARAR (1,0), LM w r performs relatively better in Table 3 than in Table 4. These results suggest that the performance of tests statistics should be investigated under realistic DGPs.

. In Table 3, LM w l performs satisfactorily regardless of the strength of spatial dependence in the alternative model and beats LM λ in all cases. In Table 3, LM gw l performs generally better than LM gA l , even though the latter requires the estimation of ρ 0 . This result may seem surprising at first, but note that in this case the least squares residuals are still consistent under the parametric misspecification of the alternative model. The relative performances of LM mw l and LM mA l are reversed, when we move from the GMM-based tests to the ML-based tests.

That is, LM mA l performs relatively better than LM mw l in most cases. In Table 4, the robust test based on the ML is performing relatively better than the one based on GMM. Also, the robust tests have relatively larger size distortions in Table 4 than in Table 3.

div.head: CONCLUSIONS
div.p: In this paper, we have formulated robust LM tests within the GMM and the ML frameworks for a social interaction model with a network structure. These tests are robust in the sense that their null asymptotic distributions are still a central chi-square distribution when the alternative model has a local parametric misspecification. We have shown that the asymptotic null distribution of the standard LM test deviates from the central chi-square distribution when the alternative model is misspecified. Hence, the robust tests are size-resistant as they produce, asymptotically, correct size. Within the context of our social interaction model, we formally showed the asymptotic distributions of our proposed tests under the null and the local alternative hypotheses. These tests can be used to test the presence of the endogenous effects, the correlated effects, and the contextual effects in a social interaction model. One attractive feature of our proposed tests is that their test statistics are easy to compute and only require the least squares estimates from a transformed linear regression model. Therefore, our proposed tests can easily be made available for practical applications using standard statistical software. In a Monte Carlo study, we investigated the size and power properties of our proposed tests. Our results showed that the robust tests have good finite sample properties and can be useful for the detection of the source of dependence in a social interaction model. The Monte Carlo results showed evidence for the analytical results that the robust tests are valid when the alternative model locally deviates from the true DGP. Of course, more simulation work and empirical applications are needed to confirm further the finite sample properties of our suggested tests.
